opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think it matters for a few reasons, and some of them are pretty practical rather than idealistic.

The first is that so much of the most important work in open models is now happening in China. If you look at the open-weight ecosystem over the last couple of years, labs like DeepSeek, Qwen, Moonshot, Zhipu, and others have been releasing really strong models with permissive licenses, and often with detailed technical reports. As someone who works on open models and post-training, I learn a ton from reading those papers and playing with those weights. If the research communities stop talking to each other, everyone loses access to ideas, and progress gets slower and more duplicated.

The second reason is about understanding. In the U.S., a lot of the conversation about Chinese AI is filtered through policy and national security framing, and some of that is warranted. But when you don't have direct relationships with the researchers, you end up with caricatures. You either overestimate or underestimate what's happening, and both are dangerous. Talking to the people actually training these models gives you a much more grounded picture of their constraints, their compute situation, their culture, and what they're optimizing for.

Third, there's a safety and norms dimension. These systems are going to be deployed globally regardless of where they're built. If we want shared expectations around things like evaluations, transparency, documentation, and responsible release, those norms have to be built with people, not just imposed through export controls or press releases. Researcher-to-researcher trust is one of the few channels that tends to survive when official relations get tense.

And honestly, part of my motivation is also a bit of a wake-up call for the U.S. I've been pretty vocal that America needs to invest more in its own open models, because right now a lot of the best open-weight models people build on are Chinese. Engaging with the Chinese community makes that really concrete. You see how fast they're moving and how much they've embraced openness, and it makes the case for why the U.S. needs a stronger open ecosystem of its own. Competition and connection aren't mutually exclusive. The healthiest version of this is one where we compete hard but still read each other's papers, share benchmarks, and keep talking.

r001.rationale: The response says people build on strong Chinese open-weight models, but it does not identify U.S. companies’ reliance on those models for products.

r002.rationale: It describes Chinese models as strong and their development as fast, but does not say that learning about China’s AI talent makes their competitiveness less surprising.

r003.rationale: The response discusses access to research and shared safety norms, but does not identify changes in how people obtain information as a societal risk of AI.

r004.rationale: It says direct relationships can prevent caricatures and give outsiders a grounded understanding of researchers, but does not distinguish those researchers from politically charged decisions they did not make.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, it comes down to the fact that this is a shared project whether we like it or not. The frontier of AI research isn't owned by one country. If you look at the author lists on the papers that actually move the field, a huge fraction of them are Chinese researchers, whether they're working in Beijing, in the Bay Area, or somewhere in between. Pretending those communities are separate is just a factual mistake about how the science happens.

The second thing is that, especially in open models, the Chinese labs have become some of the most important players. DeepSeek, Qwen, Kimi, these releases have changed how the rest of the world thinks about what's possible with open weights. I spend a lot of my time trying to understand what they're doing and why, and a lot of what I've learned has come from actually talking to people rather than reading press coverage, which tends to be pretty distorted in both directions. In the U.S. there's this tendency to either dismiss the work or treat it as some kind of threat, and neither frame helps you understand it.

And then there's the safety and governance piece. If you believe this technology is going to be consequential, and I do, then the people building it need to be able to talk to each other. Norms around evaluation, around disclosure, around what counts as responsible release, those don't get established through governments issuing statements at each other. They get established because researchers know each other, trust each other, and can pick up the phone. That infrastructure of relationships is really fragile right now, and I think it's worth a lot of effort to protect it.

The last thing I'd say is more personal. Writing about this stuff publicly, I've been surprised how many people in China read it and reach out. There's a real hunger on both sides to understand what the other side is actually thinking, not the caricature. I think that's a good instinct, and I want to feed it rather than let the politics starve it.

r003.rationale: The response does not identify changes in how people obtain information as a societal risk of AI.

r004.rationale: It says direct contact can counter caricatures and distorted views, but does not distinguish developers from politically charged decisions they did not make.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s important because we’re working on the same technology, but we often have very different pictures of what’s happening on the other side. If your understanding of Chinese AI researchers—or American AI researchers—comes entirely through headlines, it’s easy to reduce people to competitors or geopolitical actors. You miss the actual people and the questions they’re trying to solve.

Having direct relationships gives you a way to check your assumptions. You can ask, “What are you working on? What’s hard? What do you think we’re misunderstanding?” That makes the technical conversation better, but it also matters for safety. We don’t have to agree on everything to benefit from understanding each other.

And those relationships take time to build. If we wait until there’s a crisis or a really difficult decision about AI, it’s much harder to establish trust from scratch. I’d like us to preserve the ability to talk openly, even when the broader political relationship is difficult.

r003.rationale: The response refers to headlines and misunderstandings, but does not identify changes in how people obtain information as a societal risk of AI.

r004.rationale: It says headlines can reduce people to geopolitical actors and obscure who they are, but does not specify that politically charged decisions are ones those individuals did not make.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it matters because we’re working on a technology that’s going to affect everybody, and we need some shared understanding of what’s actually happening. There’s a tendency in the U.S. to talk about Chinese AI as this single, monolithic thing, and I imagine there are similar simplifications in the other direction. Talking directly to researchers helps you get past that. You understand what people are working on, what constraints they face, and where your assumptions are wrong.

That doesn’t mean ignoring competition or real disagreements about security. But you can be competitors and still have productive scientific conversations. Those relationships make it easier to assess each other’s progress accurately, exchange ideas, and potentially coordinate on risks. If we only understand each other through headlines, we’re going to make worse decisions.
